newsitem.title: UK: Labour to try to force early British election.
newsitem.headline: Labour to try to force early British election.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair said on Monday he would do all he could to force an early general election and end 17-1/2 years of Conservative rule.
He said Prime Minister John Major was presiding over a "weak, rudderless and incompetent" government whose drift was damaging Britain.
"It's time to move on. It is time to leave the tired, decaying Tories (Conservatives) behind. That is why we will do all we can to force an early election," the Labour Party leader told reporters.
The last date for the election is May 22, but Major's parliamentary position is increasingly fragile.
His overall majority in the 651-seat House of Commons fell to just one on Sunday with the death of Conservative member of parliament Barry Porter.

The majority, which stood at 21 after the last election in 1992, will be wiped out completely, assuming Labour retains the safe seat of Barnsley East in northern England left vacant by the recent death of a Labour MP.
And the Conservatives would be in a minority if Labour were to overturn Porter's majority of 8,183 in his northwest England constituency of Wirral South.
The contest for Porter's seat is likely to be held in early 1997, and far bigger Conservative margins have been swept away during the course of the present parliament.
The parliamentary arithmetic would still be in Major's favour because all the opposition parties would have to unite to vote down the Conservatives in a no-confidence vote.

Major would probably rely principally on the nine-strong Official Ulster Unionists, who already look set to save the prime minister from an embarrassing defeat on the issue of gun control within the next few weeks.
But Blair, whose party enjoys a lead of about 20 percentage points in opinion polls, said he would certainly push for a no-confidence vote if the opportunity presented itself.
"In respect of parliamentary tactics, we will pursue any tactics that are responsible," he said.

Blair was speaking at a news conference at which Labour announced that 61 percent of the party's 380,000 members had voted, by a margin of 19 to one, to endorse its pre-election blueprint "New Labour, New Life for Britain."

The draft manifesto, which bears Blair's moderate imprint, commits Labour to cut class sizes in schools, reduce hospital waiting lists, deliver swift justice for juvenile delinquents, move 250,000 young adults from welfare to work and keep inflation low.
Blair said the strong endorsement gave Labour the best possible platform in the run-up to the election.
"Today I am saying to every member of the party: 'It is time to raise our game once more. It is time to build on our success and step up a gear'," he said.

The Conservatives, who have stumbled badly in the past two weeks over policy on schools and guns, are pinning their hopes of electoral salvation on Britain's brisk economic recovery and a popular budget next month.

The cabinet will meet on Tuesday to set the level of public spending next year, which in turn will help determine the scope for tax cuts. Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke is widely expected to trim the standard rate of income tax to 23 from 24 percent.

"Just because there are one of two difficulties... it will not blow us off course. At the end of the day it is the economy that will decide who forms the next government," Conservative MP Sir Marcus Fox, one of the party's grandees, told BBC radio.
